item.description: Guangzhou-based HackerGadgets has launched a 4-in-1 Raspberry Pi HAT that offers RTL-SDR and LoRa connectivity, GPS and Beidou/GLONASS GNSS, and a PCF85063A real-time clock (RTC). The SDR part is implemented through an RTL2832U+R860 combo supporting 100 kHz to 1.74 GHz frequency and 100 kHz-28.8 MHz HF direct sampling. The HAT also features a Semtech SX1262 LoRa transceiver supporting the 860-960 MHz frequency band, 22 dBm max output power, and Meshtastic firmware. Users can select between U.FL and SMA versions depending on the type of antennas they plan to use. item.title: Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope
item.description: Dev Kapadia’s de:volt is a breadboard simulator that runs in your browser. You can place parts and wires on a breadboard, and the circuit runs live the whole time as you build it. The project aims to be as close as a real breadboard would be. It reports errors and warnings, and you can monitor pins with its built-in oscilloscope and/or multimeter. For instance, an LED with no resistor burns out, a weak battery sags under load, a motor pulls current, and a 555 on the 4-channel scope shows its timing capacitor charging and discharging. de:volt highlights: Build circuits on a virtual breadboard using the 105 parts available from the interface: resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors, LEDs, 555 timers, 74-series and CD4000 logic, EEPROMs, motor drivers, sensors, and more. Four Arduino, BBC micro:bit, and RP2040 MCU boards are also available, and you can write and run MicroPython code from the web [...] The post Web-based breadboard simulator lets you build circuits, fix errors, and monitor designs with a built-in oscilloscope appeared first on CNX Software - Embedded Systems News.

item.title: 750 MHz GigaDevice GD32H7 Cortex-M7 MCU family gets up to 9.5MB Flash, EtherCAT for industrial applications
item.description: GigaDevice adds new industrial parts to the GD32H7 series of Cortex-M7 MCUs, running at up to 750 MHz. The new lineup includes the GD32H77R for robotic joint control, GD32H78D/77D for industrial HMI applications, GD32H78E/77E for real-time motion control, and GD32H789/779 for general industrial automation. The MCUs feature up to 9728KB of on-chip Flash, 1152KB SRAM including 640KB tightly coupled memory (TCM), and hardware accelerators for mathematical operations and digital signal processing. Depending on the variant, they also integrate a MIPI DSI display interface, an EtherCAT slave controller, industrial encoder interfaces, dual Ethernet, and three CAN-FD controllers. The devices target servo drives, humanoid robots, industrial displays, CNC machines, PLCs, and digital power systems. item.description: We’ve recently written about the P4 Launcher project that offers a desktop PC-like and/or retro-gaming experience to ESP32-P4 boards with applications stored on a microSD card and loaded into PSRAM when they run. However, I’ve recently been tipped about two new projects that go even further and aim to provide a desktop OS for microcontrollers, both currently focusing on the Olimex ESP32-P4-PC board with HDMI, Ethernet, and USB ports: Sylphide OS and Bare Metal, Do Stuff (BMDS). item.title: Tektronix 1 Series low-cost DPO oscilloscopes support AI-assisted control, start at just $450
item.description: Tektronix is better known for its high-end and pricey oscilloscopes, but has now introduced the 1 Series DPO, a line of low-cost digital phosphor oscilloscopes starting at just $450, with optional AI-assisted control through the new Tek Intelligence connector. These oscilloscopes are designed for electronics testing, embedded development, education, and everyday circuit debugging. item.title: Renesas RZ/T2N Cortex-A55/R52 industrial MPU supports four-axis motor control, TSN Ethernet, EtherCAT…
item.description: Renesas RZ/T2N industrial MPU supports up to four-axis motor control and includes PWM timers, encoder interfaces, and trigonometric accelerators. It’s designed for industrial robots, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), motion controllers, and multi-axis servo drives. The MPU features up to two 1.2 GHz Arm Cortex-A55 cores for application processing and two 800 MHz Cortex-R52 cores for real-time control. It also integrates a three-port Gigabit Ethernet switch with TSN support and industrial Ethernet protocols such as EtherCAT, PROFINET RT/IRT, and EtherNet/IP. This feature set allows real-time motor control, industrial networking, and Linux applications to run on a single chip, reducing the need for separate processors. The MPU can also work as an industrial Ethernet network controller or device, depending on the application. item.title: LabWired allows engineers to test compiled firmware on simulated MCU boards (CPU and peripherals)
item.description: Andrii Shylenko’s LabWired is an MIT-licensed MCU firmware simulation core that runs compiled firmware against modeled CPUs and peripherals, captures UART and bus output, register state, and supports repeatable checks in CI. The simulator works on Arm Cortex-M0+, Cortex-M3, Cortex-M4, Cortex-M7, Cortex-M33 cores, RISC-V architecutre, and Xtensa LX6 and LX7 (some ESP32 parts). The main benefit of the project is speeding up firmware testing since doing some on real boards is slow. The hardware must be ready, then the firmware must be flashed to the board each time you want to test it, and if something breaks, developers get a dark LED and no trace. If a firmware project needs to support multiple boards, this quickly adds up. The project is different from a CPU/MCU emulator for two main reasons: The full board is modeled, not only the chip. Sensors, displays, and bus devices are also simulated.
